summary: Will Brown, a machine learning researcher at Morgan Stanley with a PhD from Columbia (co-advised by Christos Papadimitriou and Tim Roughgarden), delivers a speculative talk on reinforcement learning's role in agent development. He frames the current landscape using OpenAI's five levels: chatbots (solved), reasoners (doing well with o1, o3, R1, Grok 3, Gemini), and agents (level three, in progress). Brown distinguishes pipelines—low-autonomy, heavily engineered workflows—from true agents that interact with environments and improve over time. Most current agents like Cursor, Windsurf, and Replit have tight feedback loops; few run autonomously beyond ten minutes, with Devon, Operator, and OpenAI deep research as exceptions. Brown highlights DeepSeek R1 as the first paper explaining how to build reasoning models like o1 through RL, where long chain-of-thought reasoning emerged as a learned byproduct rather than manually programmed behavior. He explains GRPO: sample n completions per prompt, score them, reinforce higher-scoring ones—still single-turn and non-agentic. OpenAI's deep research, confirmed as end-to-end RL with up to 100 browsing tool calls, demonstrates agentic RL potential but isn't AGI. Brown then shares his viral single-file GRPO experiment training Llama 1B on math questions, which captured widespread attention for its simplicity and invited modification. He introduces 'rubric engineering'—designing reward functions that go beyond binary correctness to include format adherence, partial credit, and creative scoring rules. He notes emerging directions like using LLMs to design rubrics, autotuning with frameworks like DSPI, incorporating LM judges, and warns about reward hacking. Brown describes his open-source framework for RL in multi-step environments, where developers define interaction protocols that plug into trainers without managing weights or tokens. He concludes by sketching AI engineering in the RL era, noting that skills are hard to include in prompts (unlike knowledge) and require trial-and-error learning, that fine-tuning is reviving as open-source models close the gap with frontier models, and that building environments and rubrics directly parallels building evals and prompts—making existing AI engineering skills transferable.

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Framing
sections.summary: Will Brown introduces himself as an ML researcher at Morgan Stanley with a Columbia PhD. He clarifies the talk is speculative and forward-looking, not about proven production techniques, aiming to synthesize research trends and recent open-source work to help attendees prepare for a future where RL is part of agent engineering.

sections.title: Current State: Chatbots, Reasoners, and Agents vs. Pipelines
sections.summary: Brown uses OpenAI's five levels framework to situate current progress: chatbots and reasoners are doing well, but agents (level three) remain a work in progress. He distinguishes pipelines (low-autonomy, heavily engineered workflows) from true agents, noting most current examples like Cursor and Replit have tight feedback loops. Few agents run autonomously beyond 10 minutes, with Devon, Operator, and OpenAI deep research as exceptions.

sections.title: Model Trends and DeepSeek R1
sections.summary: Brown reviews model trends: pre-training diminishing returns, RLHF's limitations for frontier capability, and synthetic data's role in distillation. He highlights DeepSeek R1 as the first paper explaining how to build reasoning models like o1 through RL, where long chain-of-thought emerges as a learned strategy rather than manually programmed behavior.

sections.title: RL Mechanics: Explore/Exploit and GRPO
sections.summary: Brown explains RL's core explore-and-exploit principle with a code-writing example. He introduces GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), DeepSeek's algorithm: sample n completions per prompt, score them, reinforce higher-scoring ones. This remains single-turn and non-agentic; extending to autonomous multi-step systems is the challenge ahead.

sections.title: Deep Research, Infrastructure Gaps, and Open Questions
sections.summary: OpenAI's deep research, confirmed as end-to-end RL with up to 100 tool calls, demonstrates agentic RL potential but isn't AGI. Current infrastructure is mostly single-turn RLHF; no multi-step tool-calling fine-tuning APIs exist. Brown identifies open questions around cost, model size, generalization, and reward design, seeing major opportunity for open-source infrastructure and tooling companies.

sections.title: Rubric Engineering and the Viral Single-File Experiment
sections.summary: Brown shares his viral single-file GRPO experiment training Llama 1B on math questions using HuggingFace's trainer. The experiment showed self-correction behavior and characteristic response length dynamics. Its simplicity invited massive community engagement—forking, blog posts, Jupyter adaptations. Brown introduces 'rubric engineering': designing reward functions beyond binary correctness, giving partial credit for format adherence, XML structure, and integer answers. He notes emerging directions like LLM-designed rubrics, DSPI autotuning, LM judges, and warns about reward hacking.

sections.title: Open-Source Multi-Step RL Framework and the RL Era Conclusion
sections.summary: Brown describes his open-source framework for RL in multi-step environments, where developers define interaction protocols that plug into trainers without managing weights or tokens. He concludes by sketching AI engineering in the RL era: skills (unlike knowledge) are hard to put in prompts and require trial-and-error learning; fine-tuning is reviving as open-source models close the gap; and building environments and rubrics parallels building evals and prompts, making existing AI engineering skills directly transferable.
